claim: MukBEF is the Escherichia coli SMC complex that acts in chromosome segregation.
source: The Escherichia coli SMC complex, MukBEF, acts in chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about MukBEF function.

claim: MukBEF shares the distinctive architecture of other SMC complexes.
source: MukBEF shares the distinctive architecture of other SMC complexes, with one prominent difference; unlike other kleisins, MukF forms dimers through its N-terminal domain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a comparison between MukBEF and other SMC complexes.

claim: Unlike other kleisins, MukF forms dimers through its N-terminal domain.
source: MukBEF shares the distinctive architecture of other SMC complexes, with one prominent difference; unlike other kleisins, MukF forms dimers through its N-terminal domain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a distinguishing feature of MukF compared to other kleisins.

claim: A 4-helix bundle adjacent to the MukF dimerisation domain interacts functionally with the MukB coiled-coiled 'neck' adjacent to the ATPase head.
source: We show that a 4-helix bundle adjacent to the MukF dimerisation domain interacts functionally with the MukB coiled-coiled 'neck' adjacent to the ATPase head.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The interaction between the MukF 4-helix bundle and MukB neck leads to an asymmetric tripartite complex, as in other SMC complexes.
source: We propose that this interaction leads to an asymmetric tripartite complex, as in other SMC complexes.
evidence: This is proposed based on inference from the experimental data and comparison with other SMC complexes.

claim: MukF dimerisation is preserved during the interaction with the MukB neck.
source: Since MukF dimerisation is preserved during this interaction, MukF directs the formation of dimer of dimer MukBEF complexes, observed previously in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data showing that FN2 remains dimeric when bound to MukBHN.

claim: MukF directs the formation of dimer of dimer MukBEF complexes observed previously in vivo.
source: Since MukF dimerisation is preserved during this interaction, MukF directs the formation of dimer of dimer MukBEF complexes, observed previously in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the preservation of MukF dimerisation and supported by previous in vivo observations cited in the manuscript.

claim: The MukF N- and C-terminal domains stimulate MukB ATPase independently and additively.
source: The MukF N- and C-terminal domains stimulate MukB ATPase independently and additively.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ATPase assay data showing that FN2 and FC2 fragments independently activate MukB ATPase and together restore wild-type levels.

claim: Impairment of the MukF interaction with MukB in vivo leads to ATP hydrolysis-dependent release of MukBEF complexes from chromosomes.
source: We demonstrate that impairment of the MukF interaction with MukB in vivo leads to ATP hydrolysis-dependent release of MukBEF complexes from chromosomes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo experiments showing that overexpression of FN2 or FC5 leads to loss of MukBEF foci in wild-type but not in MukBEQ mutant cells.

claim: SMC complexes have important roles in managing and processing chromosomes in all domains of life.
source: SMC (Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes) complexes have important roles in managing and processing chromosomes in all domains of life (Gligoris and Löwe, 2016; Nolivos and Sherratt, 2014; Uhlmann, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The distinctive architecture of SMC proteins is conserved with the N-and C-terminal globular domains coming together to form an ATPase head.
source: The distinctive architecture of SMC proteins is conserved with the N-and C-terminal globular domains coming together to form an ATPase head and the intervening polypeptide folding upon itself to form ~50 nm long intramolecular coiled-coil arms, with a dimerisation hinge distal from the head (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SMC protein architecture and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The intervening polypeptide of SMC proteins folds upon itself to form ~50 nm long intramolecular coiled-coil arms.
source: The distinctive architecture of SMC proteins is conserved with the N-and C-terminal globular domains coming together to form an ATPase head and the intervening polypeptide folding upon itself to form ~50 nm long intramolecular coiled-coil arms, with a dimerisation hinge distal from the head (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SMC protein architecture.

claim: SMC proteins have a dimerisation hinge distal from the head.
source: The distinctive architecture of SMC proteins is conserved with the N-and C-terminal globular domains coming together to form an ATPase head and the intervening polypeptide folding upon itself to form ~50 nm long intramolecular coiled-coil arms, with a dimerisation hinge distal from the head (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SMC protein architecture.

claim: Upon ATP binding, the heads of SMC dimers engage to generate two ATPase active sites.
source: Upon ATP binding, the heads of SMC dimers engage to generate two ATPase active sites (Haering et al., 2002; Lammens et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In eukaryotes, SMC complexes are exclusively heterodimeric.
source: In eukaryotes, SMC complexes are exclusively heterodimeric, whilst those in bacteria are homodimers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SMC complex composition.

claim: In bacteria, SMC complexes are homodimers.
source: In eukaryotes, SMC complexes are exclusively heterodimeric, whilst those in bacteria are homodimers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SMC complex composition.

claim: A kleisin protein links the two ATPase heads of an SMC dimer, forming a large tripartite proteinaceous ring.
source: Nevertheless, the distinctive SMC architecture is conserved, with a kleisin protein linking the two ATPase heads of an SMC dimer, thereby forming a large tripartite proteinaceous ring (Figure 1 inset).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SMC complex architecture.

claim: Hawk proteins are present in cohesins and condensins.
source: Hawk proteins are present in cohesins and condensins, while kites are present in bacterial SMC complexes, including MukBEF, and eukaryote SMC5/6 complexes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SMC complex composition.

claim: Kites are present in bacterial SMC complexes, including MukBEF, and eukaryote SMC5/6 complexes.
source: Hawk proteins are present in cohesins and condensins, while kites are present in bacterial SMC complexes, including MukBEF, and eukaryote SMC5/6 complexes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SMC complex composition.

claim: Bacterial SMC complexes are more evolutionarily related to the SMC5/6 complexes of eukaryotes than to eukaryote cohesins and condensins.
source: This suggests that the bacterial complexes are more evolutionarily related to the SMC5/6 complexes of eukaryotes than to eukaryote cohesins and condensins.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of kite proteins in both bacterial SMC complexes and eukaryotic SMC5/6 complexes.

claim: DNA segments are topologically entrapped within SMC tripartite rings.
source: A substantial body of work has led to the hypothesis that DNA segments are topologically entrapped within these tripartite rings.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by a substantial body of work.

claim: ATP binding and hydrolysis are required for the entrapping of DNA within SMC rings.
source: ATP binding and hydrolysis are required for the entrapping of DNA within the rings, loading, and for DNA release, unloading (Arumugam et al., 2003; Çamdere et al., 2015; Cuylen et al., 2011; Gruber et al., 2003; Haering et al., 2002; Haering et al., 2008; Hu et al., 2011; Kanno et al., 2015; ; Nasmyth, 2011; Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014; Uhlmann, 2016; Wilhelm et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: E. coli and its closest γ-proteobacterial relatives encode MukBEF, an apparently distant SMC relative with little primary sequence homology to other SMCs.
source: E. coli and its closest γ-proteobacterial relatives, encode an apparently distant SMC relative, MukBEF, with little primary sequence homology to other SMCs (Nolivos and Sherratt, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Organisms encoding MukBEF have co-evolved topoisomerase IV and MatP, which interact with MukB physically and/or functionally.
source: Organisms encoding MukBEF have co-evolved a number of other distinctive proteins, some of which interact with MukB physically and/or functionally; specifically, topoisomerase IV and MatP both interact with MukB in vitro and in vivo (BrezellecBrézellec et al., 2006; Hayama and Marians, 2010; Hayama et al., 2013; Li et al., 2010; Nicolas et al., 2014; Nolivos et al., 2016; Vos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: MukB forms SMC homodimers.
source: MukB forms SMC homodimers, whereas MukF is the kleisin and MukE the kite protein that binds MukF (Palecek and Gruber, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: MukF is the kleisin in the MukBEF complex.
source: MukB forms SMC homodimers, whereas MukF is the kleisin and MukE the kite protein that binds MukF (Palecek and Gruber, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: MukE is the kite protein that binds MukF.
source: MukB forms SMC homodimers, whereas MukF is the kleisin and MukE the kite protein that binds MukF (Palecek and Gruber, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: All three proteins of the MukBEF complex (MukB, MukE, and MukF) are required for function.
source: All three proteins of the MukBEF complex are required for function, and their impairment leads to defects in chromosome segregation, manifested by impairment of segregation of newly replicated origins (ori) and mis-orientation of chromosomes with respect to their genetic map within cells (Danilova et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Impairment of MukBEF proteins leads to defects in chromosome segregation.
source: All three proteins of the MukBEF complex are required for function, and their impairment leads to defects in chromosome segregation, manifested by impairment of segregation of newly replicated origins (ori) and mis-orientation of chromosomes with respect to their genetic map within cells (Danilova et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: In rich media, MukBEF impairment leads to inviability at higher temperatures and formation of anucleate cells during permissive low-temperature growth.
source: In rich media, this leads to inviability at higher temperatures and formation of anucleate cells during permissive low-temperature growth (Niki et al., 1991; Yamanaka et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Most SMC complexes bind their cognate monomeric kleisins asymmetrically.
source: Where characterised, most SMC complexes bind their cognate monomeric kleisins asymmetrically, with their N-terminal regions binding the SMC 'neck' adjacent to the ATPase head of the molecule distal to the molecule binding the kleisin C-terminus, thereby-forming the tripartite protein ring (Figure 1 inset) (Bürmann et al., 2013; Gligoris et al., 2014; Gligoris and Löwe, 2016; Gruber et al., 2003; Haering et al., 2004; Huis in't Veld et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by multiple citations.

claim: In most SMC complexes, kleisin N-terminal regions bind the SMC 'neck' adjacent to the ATPase head of the molecule distal to the molecule binding the kleisin C-terminus.
source: Where characterised, most SMC complexes bind their cognate monomeric kleisins asymmetrically, with their N-terminal regions binding the SMC 'neck' adjacent to the ATPase head of the molecule distal to the molecule binding the kleisin C-terminus, thereby-forming the tripartite protein ring (Figure 1 inset) (Bürmann et al., 2013; Gligoris et al., 2014; Gligoris and Löwe, 2016; Gruber et al., 2003; Haering et al., 2004; Huis in't Veld et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by multiple citations.

claim: MukF forms stable dimers through interacting N-terminal winged-helix domains (WHD).
source: MukF is an atypical kleisin, in that it forms stable dimers through interacting N-terminal winged-helix domains (WHD), while its C-terminal domain interacts with the MukB head at the cap, as is the case for characterised SMC kleisins (Fennell-Fezzie et al., 2005; Woo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The MukF C-terminal domain interacts with the MukB head at the cap.
source: MukF is an atypical kleisin, in that it forms stable dimers through interacting N-terminal winged-helix domains (WHD), while its C-terminal domain interacts with the MukB head at the cap, as is the case for characterised SMC kleisins (Fennell-Fezzie et al., 2005; Woo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: One MukB dimer is expected to bind a MukF dimer and two MukE dimers in the absence of ATP.
source: Therefore, one MukB dimer is expected to bind a MukF dimer and two MukE dimers in the absence of ATP (Figure 1A); ATP binding leads to head dimerisation, accompanied by steric expulsion of one of the two MukF C-terminal domains and head engagement (Woo et al., 2009, Figure 1B left panel).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural properties of MukF and supported by a citation.

claim: ATP binding leads to MukB head dimerisation, accompanied by steric expulsion of one of the two MukF C-terminal domains and head engagement.
source: Therefore, one MukB dimer is expected to bind a MukF dimer and two MukE dimers in the absence of ATP (Figure 1A); ATP binding leads to head dimerisation, accompanied by steric expulsion of one of the two MukF C-terminal domains and head engagement (Woo et al., 2009, Figure 1B left panel).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: The interaction between the MukF N-terminal domain and the MukB neck is required for MukBEF function in vivo.
source: We show that this interaction with the MukB neck is required for MukBEF function in vivo, and infer that this interaction is established and broken during cycles of ATP binding and hydrolysis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo complementation assays showing that MukF and MukB variants with impaired neck-N-terminal domain interactions fail to complement temperature-sensitive growth defects.

claim: The interaction between the MukF N-terminal domain and the MukB neck is established and broken during cycles of ATP binding and hydrolysis.
source: We show that this interaction with the MukB neck is required for MukBEF function in vivo, and infer that this interaction is established and broken during cycles of ATP binding and hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that overexpression of FN2 leads to ATP hydrolysis-dependent loss of MukBEF clusters.

claim: Each of the MukF N-terminal and C-terminal domain ATPase activities is inhibited by MukE.
source: Interactions of the MukF N-terminal domain with the MukB neck and MukF C-terminal domain with the MukB head, activate MukB ATPase independently and additively in vitro, with the addition of both fragments restoring wild type MukB ATPase levels. Each of these ATPase activities was inhibited by MukE, with the inhibition being relieved in the presence of DNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase assays showing that MukE inhibits MukB ATPase activated by FN2, FN10, and FC2 fragments.

claim: MukE inhibition of MukB ATPase is relieved in the presence of DNA.
source: Each of these ATPase activities was inhibited by MukE, with the inhibition being relieved in the presence of DNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase assays showing that addition of DNA restores MukB ATPase activity in the presence of MukE.

claim: Interaction of the MukF N-terminal domain with the MukB neck did not compromise MukF dimerisation.
source: We show that interaction of the MukF N-terminal domain with the MukB neck did not compromise MukF dimerisation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-MALS data showing that FN2 remains dimeric when bound to MukBHN.

claim: MukF dimerisation in heads-engaged MukBEF complexes directs formation of dimers of MukBEF dimers.
source: Therefore, MukF dimerisation in heads-engaged MukBEF complexes directs formation of dimers of MukBEF dimers, thereby explaining the stoichiometry observed in vivo (Badrinarayanan et al., 2012a, Figure 1B right panel).
evidence: This is inferred from the preservation of MukF dimerisation during interaction with MukB neck and supported by previous in vivo stoichiometry measurements.

claim: MukF C-terminal derivatives FC1 and FC2 interacted with MukB and all of its derivatives (MukBH and MukBHN).
source: MukF C-terminal derivatives, FC1 and FC2, interacted with MukB, and all of its derivatives, as expected, because the MukB ATPase head participates in this interaction (Figure 2B; Figure 1; Woo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: FN2, containing the N-terminal dimerisation WHD and an adjacent 4-helix bundle, interacted strongly with intact MukB and MukBHN, but not with MukBH.
source: FN2, containing the N-terminal dimerisation WHD and an adjacent 4-helix bundle, interacted strongly with intact MukB and MukBHN, but not with MukBH, consistent with FN2 interacting with the MukB neck (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: FN1, containing just the WHD involved in MukF dimerisation, did not interact with MukB derivatives.
source: We detected no interactions of FN1, containing just the WHD involved in MukF dimerisation, with the MukB derivatives.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down assays.

claim: FN3, containing the 4-helix bundle (helices 6–9), interacted with MukB and MukBHN, but not MukBH.
source: In contrast, FN3, containing the 4-helix bundle (helices 6–9), and FN4, carrying only helices 8 and 9, interacted with MukB and MukBHN, but not MukBH (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: FN4, carrying only helices 8 and 9, interacted with MukB and MukBHN, but not MukBH.
source: In contrast, FN3, containing the 4-helix bundle (helices 6–9), and FN4, carrying only helices 8 and 9, interacted with MukB and MukBHN, but not MukBH (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: FN6, lacking helices 8 and 9, failed to interact with MukBHN.
source: Consistent with this, FN6 lacking helices 8 and 9 failed to show an interaction in size exclusion chromatography-multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) assays (below) and FN7, lacking helix 9 failed to interact with MukBHN (Figure 2B bottom right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-MALS assays and pull-down assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: FN7, lacking helix 9, failed to interact with MukBHN.
source: Consistent with this, FN6 lacking helices 8 and 9 failed to show an interaction in size exclusion chromatography-multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) assays (below) and FN7, lacking helix 9 failed to interact with MukBHN (Figure 2B bottom right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Helices 8 and 9 of the 4-helix bundle are sufficient for interaction with the MukB neck.
source: We conclude that while helices 8 and 9 of the 4-helix bundle are sufficient for interaction with the MukB neck, helix 9 is essential.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that FN4 (containing only helices 8 and 9) interacts with MukBHN, while FN7 (lacking helix 9) does not.

claim: Helix 9 is essential for interaction with the MukB neck.
source: We conclude that while helices 8 and 9 of the 4-helix bundle are sufficient for interaction with the MukB neck, helix 9 is essential.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that FN7 (lacking helix 9) fails to interact with MukBHN.

claim: MukBHN was monomeric in solution.
source: MukBHN was monomeric in solution, while FN2 was dimeric, as expected from structural analyses (Fennell-Fezzie et al., 2005; Woo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-MALS analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: FN2 was dimeric in solution.
source: MukBHN was monomeric in solution, while FN2 was dimeric, as expected from structural analyses (Fennell-Fezzie et al., 2005; Woo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-MALS analysis shown in Figure 3 and is consistent with previous structural analyses.

claim: When MukBHN and FN2 were mixed at a molar ratio of 1 MukBHN monomer:1.25 FN2 dimer, two additional peaks of masses 165 kDa and 284 kDa were evident in addition to the MukBHN monomers.
source: When mixed at a molar ratio of 1 MukBHN monomer:1.25 2FN2 (in the figures, we refer to FN2 dimers as 2FN2, to reflect their dimeric state), two additional peaks of masses 165 kDa and 284 kDa were evident in addition to the MukBHN monomers (Figure 3A left panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-MALS analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 165 kDa and 284 kDa complexes are interpreted as complexes in which either one or two MukBHN molecules bound independently to a single FN2 dimer.
source: We interpret these as complexes in which either one or two MukBHN molecules bound independently to a single FN2 dimer.
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular masses of the complexes observed by SEC-MALS.

claim: More of the larger MukBHN-FN2 complexes were observed at higher MukBHN to FN2 ratios (3:1).
source: Consistent with this interpretation, more of the larger complexes were observed at higher MukBHN to 2FN2 ratios (3:1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-MALS analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The interaction between the MukF N-terminal domain and the MukB neck does not compromise MukF dimerisation.
source: Therefore, the interaction between the MukF N-terminal domain and the MukB neck does not compromise MukF dimerisation.
evidence: This is concluded from SEC-MALS data showing that FN2 remains dimeric when bound to MukBHN.

claim: Binding of the second MukBHN to MukBHN-FN2 complex may be less favourable than binding of the first MukBHN to FN2.
source: The relatively low proportion of complexes of stoichiometry MukBHN-2FN2-MukBHN as compared to MukBHN-2FN2 in the presence of a large excess of MukBHN, indicates that binding of the second MukBHN to MukBHN-2FN2 complex may be less favourable than binding of the first MukBHN to FN2.
evidence: This is inferred from the relative proportions of different complexes observed by SEC-MALS.

claim: FC2, but not FN2, formed complexes with MukBH.
source: In agreement with the Flag-MukF-MukB interaction assays, FC2, but not FN2, formed complexes with MukBH (Figure 3A middle and right panels).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-MALS analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Addition of ATP did not significantly alter the nature or abundance of complexes containing MukBHN and FN2 or FC2.
source: Addition of ATP did not significantly alter the nature or abundance of complexes containing MukBHN and FN2 or FC2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-MALS analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: MukBHN is unable to form stable heads-engaged dimers with either FN2 or FC2 in the presence of ATP.
source: This is consistent with MukBHN, which is a monomer in solution, being unable to form stable heads-engaged dimers with either FN2 or FC2 in the presence of ATP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ATP does not alter the complexes formed between MukBHN and FN2 or FC2.

claim: Mixtures of MukBHN, FN2 and FC2 yielded larger complexes than those formed with MukBHN and FN2 alone.
source: SEC analysis (Figure 3C) showed that mixtures of MukBHN, FN2 and FC2 yielded larger complexes (olive green trace) than those formed with MukBHN and FN2 alone (dark green trace), consistent with binding of both FN2 and FC2 to a single monomer of MukBHN.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both FN2 and FC2 can bind simultaneously to a single monomer of MukBHN.
source: SEC analysis (Figure 3C) showed that mixtures of MukBHN, FN2 and FC2 yielded larger complexes (olive green trace) than those formed with MukBHN and FN2 alone (dark green trace), consistent with binding of both FN2 and FC2 to a single monomer of MukBHN.
evidence: This is inferred from SEC analysis showing larger complexes when both FN2 and FC2 are present.

claim: A complex containing a MukB dimer with unengaged heads, bound to a MukF dimer may be stabilised by MukF interactions to both the MukB head and neck.
source: Therefore, a complex containing a MukB dimer with unengaged heads, bound to a MukF dimer may be stabilised by MukF interactions to both the MukB head and neck.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both FN2 and FC2 can bind simultaneously to a single MukBHN monomer.

claim: An equivalent result of simultaneous binding of kleisin N- and C-terminal domains to a single SMC molecule was observed with B. subtilis SMC complexes.
source: An equivalent result was observed with B. subtilis SMC complexes, with both head and neck of a single SMC molecule being bound simultaneously by kleisin N-and C-terminal domains (Bürmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on B. subtilis SMC complexes.

claim: Both MukF N-terminal and C-terminal domains bound to MukB with similar affinities, with Kds in the 9–26 nM range.
source: Both domains bound to MukB with similar affinities, with Kds in the 9–26 nM range, suggesting that interactions of the N-terminal and C-terminal MukF domains with the MukB neck and head, respectively, are similarly strong (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FCS and FPA measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: FN10, which in addition to the N-terminal domain also carries the MukF middle region, bound more tightly to MukB than FN2.
source: FN10, which in addition to the N-terminal domain also carries the MukF middle region, bound more tightly to MukB than FN2, consistent with the MukF middle region interacting directly with MukB (Woo et al., 2009)
evidence: This is demonstrated by FCS measurements and is consistent with previous structural studies.

claim: MukB dimers alone had negligible ATPase activity.
source: MukB dimers alone had negligible ATPase activity (Figure 4), in agreement with previous reports (Petrushenko et.al., 2005; Woo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase assays shown in Figure 4 and is consistent with previous reports.

claim: Addition of MukF kleisin led to robust MukB ATPase.
source: Addition of MukF kleisin led to robust MukB ATPase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: The steady state ATPase rate was ~21 ATP molecules hydrolysed/min/MukB dimer under conditions of MukF excess.
source: The steady state ATPase rate was ~21 ATP molecules hydrolysed/min/MukB dimer, under conditions of MukF excess (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MukF alone did not exhibit ATPase activity.
source: MukF alone did not exhibit ATPase activity.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from ATPase assays.

claim: Both FN2 and FC2 variants stimulated MukB ATPase.
source: To dissect the MukF requirements for MukB ATPase, we assayed two MukF truncations, containing either the N-terminal domain (FN2), or the C-terminal domain and the middle region (FC2) (Figure 2A). Both variants stimulated MukB ATPase (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Saturating FC2, at a 2.5-fold molar excess, gave 60% of the maximal ATPase obtained with MukF.
source: Saturating FC2, at a 2.5-fold molar excess, gave 60% of the maximal ATPase obtained with MukF, while saturating FN2 (at a 2.5-fold molar excess) gave 33% of maximum ATPase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1BC), while a truncation equivalent to FN2 plus the MukF middle region raised this level to ~50% (later).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1BC.

claim: Saturating FN2 (at a 2.5-fold molar excess) gave 33% of maximum ATPase.
source: Saturating FC2, at a 2.5-fold molar excess, gave 60% of the maximal ATPase obtained with MukF, while saturating FN2 (at a 2.5-fold molar excess) gave 33% of maximum ATPase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1BC), while a truncation equivalent to FN2 plus the MukF middle region raised this level to ~50% (later).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1BC.

claim: Addition of FN2 and FC2 together restored ATPase to the level observed with wild type MukF.
source: Addition of FN2 and FC2 together restored ATPase to the level observed with wild type MukF.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: FN6, lacking helices 8 and 9, did not stimulate MukB ATPase.
source: FN6, lacking helices 8 and 9, did not stimulate MukB ATPase, consistent with its failure to interact with the MukB neck (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: MukB ATPase is activated additively and independently by the N-and C-terminal domains of MukF, with each domain being able to activate ~50% of maximal MukB ATPase.
source: Taken together, the results show that MukB ATPase is activated additively and independently by the N-and C-terminal domains of MukF, with each domain being able to activate ~50% of maximal MukB ATPase.
evidence: This is concluded from ATPase assays showing that FN2 and FC2 independently activate MukB ATPase and together restore wild-type levels.

claim: Three variants with triple substitutions in helix 9 of FN2 (FN2m1, FN2m2, and FN2m3) exhibited an impaired ability to activate MukB ATPase.
source: Three variants with triple substitutions in helix 9 of FN2 exhibited an impaired ability to activate MukB ATPase. FN2m2 (substitutions R279E K283A R286A) displayed a ~10 fold reduction in the ability to activate MukB ATPase, FN2m3 (D261K S265K Q268A), showed a ~2 fold reduction, while FN2m1 (D272K I275K R279D) was reduced by about a third (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: FN2m1 and FN2m2 failed to interact detectably with MukBHN.
source: Moreover, SEC analysis showed that FN2m1 and FN2m2 failed to interact detectably with MukBHN (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither MukFm2 nor MukFm3 could complement the temperature-sensitivity of ΔmukF cells.
source: Consistent with these results, functional in vivo complementation analysis of the ability of full length MukF variants, containing these sets of mutations, showed that neither MukFm2 nor MukFm3 could complement the temperature-sensitivity of ΔmukF cells, while MukFm1 exhibited partial complementation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo complementation assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: MukFm1 exhibited partial complementation of the temperature-sensitivity of ΔmukF cells.
source: Consistent with these results, functional in vivo complementation analysis of the ability of full length MukF variants, containing these sets of mutations, showed that neither MukFm2 nor MukFm3 could complement the temperature-sensitivity of ΔmukF cells, while MukFm1 exhibited partial complementation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo complementation assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: MukBm3 (L1219K L1226K) had about 35% of wild type ATPase activity when activated by full length MukF.
